content: This information is critical because many pregnant women require medical treatment for conditions that either arise or persist during pregnancy. Certain medications are known to increase the risk of structural congenital malformations and other adverse pregnancy or developmental outcomes. Both healthcare providers and pregnant women must carefully weigh the risks of continuing a treatment during pregnancy against the risks of discontinuing it, which could lead to the recurrence or worsening of the medical condition. Either scenario could pose a risk to the fetus. Teratology information databases are developed by research groups that specifically study the effects of pharmaceuticals and, in some cases, chemicals on pregnancy outcomes. These databases provide evidence-based evaluations to support risk assessments related to chemical exposures or the use of medications and vaccines during pregnancy. Some databases are focused on guiding decisions about the safest choices of medications and vaccines for use during pregnancy, particularly when their safety profiles are uncertain. In Australia, the Therapeutic Goods Administration offers the Prescribing Medicines in Pregnancy database on an open-access website. This resource is designed to assist healthcare professionals in planning the medical management of pregnant patients or those intending to become pregnant. Additionally, the Royal Hospital for Women in Randwick, New South Wales, provides a website with fact sheets on exposures during pregnancy and breastfeeding. In Europe, the European Network of Teratology Information Services hosts a website that directs users to teratology information summaries. This site also provides contact details for teratology information specialists in the user’s geographical area. Despite being labeled as a European network, it includes member centers in Australia, Japan, and South America. Examples of teratology information databases in Europe include: In France, the Reference Centre on Teratogenic Agents provides information on the risks of drugs, vaccines, radiation, and addiction during pregnancy and breastfeeding, though it is available only in French. In Germany, Embryotox offers up-to-date scientific information on over 400 medications, available only in German, with smartphone applications also provided. In the Netherlands, the Pharmacovigilance Centre Lareb provides information in both English and Dutch. In the United Kingdom, the Teratology Information Service offers two open-access databases with summaries of over 350 drug and chemical exposures during pregnancy. One of these databases, called Best Use of Medicines in Pregnancy (BUMPS), is written specifically for the general public and provides plain-English fact sheets on common drugs and some chemicals. More detailed, fully referenced monographs are available for registered UK healthcare professionals through TOXBASE. In North America, the Organization of Teratology Information Specialists hosts the MotherToBaby website, which provides expert information about exposures during pregnancy and breastfeeding in both English and Spanish. General toxicology resources are also available online or through smartphone applications. These resources compile information on chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and other substances. Some are commercial databases requiring subscriptions, while others are free resources provided by national or international organizations. Examples include publications from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the International Agency for Research on Cancer, the World Health Organization (WHO), and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). These organizations publish toxicological evaluations of high-priority chemicals, which are accessible free of charge on their websites. WHO publishes the Environmental Health Criteria series and Concise International Chemical Assessment Documents, which evaluate chemicals' effects on human health and the environment. WHO also provides guidelines for drinking-water quality, including chemical fact sheets and supporting documents. Additionally, WHO and FAO jointly publish toxicological assessments of food additives, contaminants, and pesticide residues, including information on acceptable daily intakes. The International Agency for Research on Cancer publishes monographs on identifying carcinogenic hazards to humans, offering reliable, up-to-date information on numerous chemicals. The secretariats of the Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions (FAO and UNEP) compile toxicological information on industrial chemicals and pesticides under consideration for listing in these conventions. The OECD provides Screening Information Datasets on selected high-production-volume chemicals, including toxicity data reviews, and offers access to intergovernmental information through the eChemPortal. Each poison center should maintain documentation relevant to its country or region, ideally in the local language(s). Essential resources include indexes and guides of medicines and chemicals, standard medical textbooks, current awareness bulletins, and journals on medicine and toxicology. Many journals are available online, with some free of charge and others requiring subscriptions. The HINARI program, established by WHO and major publishers, enables lowand middle-income countries to access biomedical and health journals, including toxicology journals, at low or no cost. Bibliographic databases such as Medline/PubMed, TOXLINE, and others provide access to abstracts and bibliographic indexes. WHO’s Global Index Medicus offers universal access to biomedical and public health literature from lowand middle-income countries. Other electronic resources, such as DSpace, Koha, and Greenstone Digital Library Software, can help poison center libraries manage collections of papers and publications. The eGranary Digital Library provides offline access to millions of internet resources, useful in settings with limited internet connectivity. In conclusion, high-quality information resources are essential for the effective operation of poison centers. While electronic resources offer rapid searching and compact storage, paper-based resources remain valuable, particularly in low-resource settings. Many databases, books, and journals are costly, but free or low-cost access is often available for academic and health institutions in lowand middle-income countries.
